title: Tests Of Uniformity And Goodness-Of-Fit
notes: Open the lecture by naming uniformity as the circular null model that everything else has to respect. The important geometric constraint is that the zero angle is a coordinate choice, not a property of the data. Preview the chapter as a set of diagnostic lenses: mean vectors, circular empirical distribution functions, spacings, semicircles, pairwise kernels, and probability integral transforms.

title: Uniformity Means No Direction Survives Rotation
notes: Use the unit-circle schematic to separate the statistical claim from the coordinate system. Under uniformity, rotating the origin should not change the evidence, and every nonzero harmonic has zero population resultant. This is why circular tests must either be explicitly invariant or make clear which geometric feature they are designed to detect.

title: A Test Family Is A Diagnostic Map
notes: Frame the chapter as a map rather than a ranking of tests. Rayleigh is local to the first harmonic, Kuiper and Watson are empirical-distribution scans, spacing and Ajne tests look at gaps and semicircles, Hermans-Rasson and Beran use pairwise or integrated discrepancies, and PIT diagnostics convert model checking back into uniformity checking.

title: Rayleigh Reads The First Harmonic
notes: Present Rayleigh as the cleanest geometry in the chapter: add the unit vectors and ask whether the resultant is too long. The notebook example makes the limitation visible. A unimodal sample gives a large first resultant, while a symmetric antipodal pattern can be strikingly nonuniform and still cancel almost perfectly in the first harmonic.

title: The Rayleigh Blind Spot Is Harmonic
notes: Use the harmonic panel to explain why Rayleigh is powerful but not omnibus. The first resultant is tuned to one preferred direction. When mass appears in opposite lobes, the first vectors cancel but the doubled angles align. That observation motivates second-harmonic diagnostics and warns students not to equate a large Rayleigh p-value with uniformity.

title: CDF Tests Must Survive The Cut
notes: Move from vectors to empirical distribution functions by emphasizing the artificial cut. The step function depends on where zero is placed, so raw one-sided discrepancies move when the origin moves. Kuiper combines the positive and negative excursions, and Watson recenters the squared discrepancy, leaving the statistic stable under rotation.

title: Kuiper And Watson Keep Different Shape Memory
notes: The two formulas should be read as design choices. Kuiper keeps the largest upward and downward gaps, so it is sensitive to localized departures anywhere around the circle. Watson integrates squared discrepancy after removing the mean offset, so it behaves like a smooth global CDF energy. Both avoid rewarding a convenient origin.

title: Spacings Ask Where The Circle Is Empty
notes: Spacing tests do not begin with a preferred direction or a CDF curve; they begin with ordered gaps. A cluster creates a large empty arc and several unusually small adjacent gaps. In the notebook artifact, the largest gap is about eighty-three degrees and the covering arc is about two hundred seventy-seven degrees, which is a geometric signature rather than a single-vector signal.

title: Ajne Scans Every Semicircle
notes: Use Ajne-style semicircle scanning as the bridge between spacing and distribution-function thinking. If the data are uniform, a moving half-circle should usually contain about half the observations. Too many or too few points in some semicircle signals hemispheric imbalance, and the scan stays circular because every possible center is considered.

title: Hermans-Rasson And Beran Use Pairwise Energy
notes: Introduce these omnibus tests qualitatively because their value is not a new picture of the origin but a new object of comparison. They score the whole interpoint-separation fingerprint against what uniformity would produce. Pairwise kernels can see multimodal or axial structure that a first-harmonic resultant may miss, while integrated discrepancy tests average evidence around the circle.

title: PIT Turns Model Fit Into Uniformity
notes: For goodness-of-fit, shift the null from a uniform circle to a specified continuous circular model. The probability integral transform maps each observation through the fitted or hypothesized circular CDF, then wraps the result back to an angle. If the model is adequate, those transformed angles should pass the same uniformity diagnostics.

title: Null Envelopes Reveal Failure Modes
notes: Use the simulation envelopes as calibration rather than as a replacement for analytic critical values. The unimodal alternative trips nearly every statistic, the antipodal alternative defeats Rayleigh while stressing Watson and spacing diagnostics, and the cluster-with-gap alternative is most visible to spacing-sensitive summaries. The point is to match test geometry to alternative geometry.

title: A Compact Report Keeps The Tests Honest
notes: The applied report is the practical endpoint of the chapter. Instead of announcing one omnibus p-value, the report lists which geometric features were measured and whether they were origin invariant. The example has significant Rayleigh, Kuiper, Watson, and spacing evidence, plus ranges showing that Kuiper and Watson remain stable as the cut moves.

title: Choose The Test From The Alternative
notes: Turn the lecture into a decision workflow. A single preferred direction calls for Rayleigh. General CDF deviations call for Kuiper or Watson. Empty arcs and clustered spacings call for Rao, Ajne, or related spacing scans. Symmetric multimodal structure calls for higher harmonics or energy tests. Model adequacy calls for PIT followed by uniformity diagnostics.

title: Common Misreads
notes: Pause on mistakes because this chapter is full of plausible but wrong shortcuts. A nonsignificant Rayleigh statistic is not proof of uniformity. A CDF plot drawn from one origin is not a circular statistic by itself. A fitted PIT diagnostic must remember that parameters were estimated. A useful test report names the geometry it is capable of seeing.

title: Uniformity Testing Checklist
notes: Close with an operational checklist students can apply to a new circular sample. Plot the data first, ask whether the origin matters, compute a first-harmonic test, add origin-invariant CDF summaries, inspect gaps and semicircle counts, use energy or higher-harmonic checks for multimodal alternatives, and use the PIT when the null is a fitted circular model.
